items.stem: Which instrument is used to measure lung volumes?
items.answer: a spirometer
items.markingKey: a spirometer. Spirometers record volume changes over time.

items.stem: Why do premature babies sometimes develop breathing difficulties?
options: Type II pneumocytes may not yet produce enough surfactant, so alveoli collapse.
items.answer: Type II pneumocytes may not yet produce enough surfactant, so alveoli collapse.
items.markingKey: C. Surfactant is produced late in gestation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Gas exchange happens in the bronchi and trachea." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Gas exchange occurs across the alveolar walls; the airways only conduct air.
items.markingKey: Gas exchange occurs across the alveolar walls; the airways only conduct air. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A spirometer trace was recorded for Yusuf, a 17-year-old student, at rest. Values read from the trace are shown.

Lung volume | Value / dm³
tidal volume | 0.46
inspiratory reserve volume | 2.32
expiratory reserve volume | 1.25
residual volume (estimated) | 1.28

During the recording Yusuf took 13 breaths in one minute.

(a) Calculate the vital capacity. [2]
(b) Calculate the ventilation rate at rest. [1]
items.answer: (a) 4.03 dm³ (b) 5.98 dm³ min⁻¹

items.stem: A student’s tidal volume is 0.5 dm³ and breathing rate 15 breaths min⁻¹. During exercise, tidal volume rises to 2.0 dm³ and rate to 30 min⁻¹. By what factor does ventilation rate increase?
items.markingKey: D. 7.5 → 60 dm³ min⁻¹.

items.stem: Briefly describe emphysema in long-term smokers and explain what it reveals about the importance of alveolar structure for gas exchange.
items.answer: Elastase from inflammatory cells breaks down elastin in alveolar walls, which merge into large air spaces. Reduced surface area and loss of elastic recoil lower the efficiency of gas exchange and ventilation.
items.markingKey: Context (Elastase from inflammatory cells breaks down elastin in alveolar walls, which merge into large air spaces.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Reduced surface area and loss of elastic recoil lower the efficiency of gas exchange and ventilation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of alveolar structure for gas exchange.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Lung capacity is the most important factor determining athletic performance."
items.answer: Lung capacity contributes, but cardiovascular and muscular factors usually limit aerobic performance more.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: larger vital capacity allows greater ventilation at high work rates; some elite rowers and swimmers have exceptional lung volumes. Arguments against: in healthy people oxygen uptake is usually limited by cardiac output and muscle capillarity, not ventilation; training improves heart and muscle far more than lung volume. Supported judgement: Lung capacity contributes, but cardiovascular and muscular factors usually limit aerobic performance more.

items.stem: Explain the mechanism of ventilation and the adaptations of the lungs for efficient gas exchange.
items.answer: Inspiration: diaphragm and external intercostals contract, volume up, pressure down, air in; expiration: relax, recoil, internal intercostals in forced; antagonistic muscles. Adaptations: large SA, thin pneumocytes, moist, capillaries, surfactant, ventilation maintains gradient; measured by spirometer.
items.markingKey: Inspiration: diaphragm and external intercostals contract, volume up, pressure down, air in; expiration: relax, recoil, internal intercostals in forced; antagonistic muscles. Adaptations: large SA, thin pneumocytes, moist, capillaries, surfactant, ventilation maintains gradient; measured by spirometer.

items.stem: Explain how the mechanism of ventilation causes air to enter the lungs.
items.answer: External intercostal muscles contract, moving the ribcage up and out; the diaphragm contracts and flattens; thorax volume increases; pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure; air flows in until pressures are equal.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: External intercostal muscles contract, moving the ribcage up and out; the diaphragm contracts and flattens; thorax volume increases; pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure; air flows in until pressures are equal. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between vital capacity and tidal volume.
items.answer: Tidal volume is the volume exchanged in a normal breath (about 0.5 dm³); vital capacity is the maximum volume exhaled after maximum inhalation (about 4–5 dm³).
items.markingKey: Tidal volume is the volume exchanged in a normal breath (about 0.5 dm³); vital capacity is the maximum volume exhaled after maximum inhalation (about 4–5 dm³). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kwame’s tidal volume at rest was 0.47 dm³ at 14 breaths per minute. During exercise it was 1.5 dm³ at 25 breaths per minute. Calculate the ventilation rate in each case and the percentage increase, and explain why it increases.
items.answer: 6.58 → 37.5 dm³ min⁻¹; +470 %; respiration in muscles increases, so more CO₂ must be removed and more O₂ supplied – rising blood CO₂ is detected by chemoreceptors, which increase breathing rate and depth
items.markingKey: 6.58 and 37.5 dm³ min⁻¹ (A1 A1); (37.5 − 6.58)/6.58 × 100 = 470 % (A1); more CO₂ from respiration detected by chemoreceptors, more O₂ needed (R1).

items.stem:
A spirometer trace was recorded for Leila, a 17-year-old student, at rest. Values read from the trace are shown.

Lung volume | Value / dm³
tidal volume | 0.52
inspiratory reserve volume | 2.45
expiratory reserve volume | 1.16
residual volume (estimated) | 1.27

During the recording Leila took 15 breaths in one minute.

(a) Calculate the vital capacity. [2]
(b) Calculate the ventilation rate at rest. [1]
(c) Calculate the total lung capacity and the percentage of it that is residual volume. [2]
(d) Explain why residual volume cannot be measured with a simple spirometer. [1]
(e) Predict and explain how tidal volume and breathing rate would change during vigorous exercise. [3]
(f) State two precautions needed when using a spirometer. [2]
(g) Suggest why vital capacity is often lower in smokers. [1]
items.answer: (a) 4.13 dm³ (b) 7.80 dm³ min⁻¹ (c) 5.40 dm³; 24 % (d) It is the air that remains in the lungs after maximum expiration, so it never enters or leaves the spirometer. (e) Both increase; tidal volume uses part of the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes; to supply more O₂ and remove more CO₂ produced by respiration. (f) Sterilise the mouthpiece; use a nose clip; ensure soda lime is fresh to absorb CO₂; stop if dizzy; person must be healthy (no asthma). (g) Damage to alveolar walls (emphysema) and narrowing of airways reduces elastic recoil and the volume that can be exhaled.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] VC = TV + IRV + ERV = 0.52 + 2.45 + 1.16 (M1) = 4.13 dm³ (A1). (b) [1] 0.52 × 15 = 7.80 dm³ min⁻¹ (A1). (c) [2] 4.13 + 1.27 = 5.40 (A1); 1.27/5.40 × 100 = 24 % (A1). (d) [1] Air never exhaled (A1). (e) [3] Both increase (A1); reserve volumes used (A1); link to respiration/CO₂ (R1). (f) [2] Two valid precautions (A1 A1). (g) [1] Valid reason (A1).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "spongy mesophyll".
items.answer: Loosely packed leaf cells with large air spaces that allow diffusion of gases to and from photosynthesising cells
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: loosely packed leaf cells with large air spaces that allow diffusion of gases to and from photosynthesising cells. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "Plants transpire mainly to cool themselves down." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Transpiration is largely an unavoidable consequence of stomata being open for CO₂ uptake; it also helps transport water and minerals and cools leaves.
items.markingKey: Transpiration is largely an unavoidable consequence of stomata being open for CO₂ uptake; it also helps transport water and minerals and cools leaves. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how temperature affects the rate of transpiration.
items.answer: Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, so evaporation from mesophyll cell walls and diffusion of water vapour out through stomata are faster; warm air holds more water vapour, so the gradient is steeper. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, so evaporation from mesophyll cell walls and diffusion of water vapour out through stomata are faster; warm air holds more water vapour, so the gradient is steeper. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Stomata were counted in five fields of view on a nail-varnish impression of the lower epidermis of a maize leaf: 11, 40, 34, 15, 18. The diameter of the field of view was 0.3 mm. Calculate the mean stomatal density in stomata per mm².
items.answer: 334 mm⁻²

items.stem: Using marram grass (Ammophila arenaria) on sand dunes as an example, explain adaptations that reduce transpiration.
items.answer: Its leaves roll up in dry conditions with stomata in pits on the inner surface, surrounded by hairs. Trapped humid air reduces the water vapour gradient, so less water is lost while some gas exchange continues.
items.markingKey: Context (Its leaves roll up in dry conditions with stomata in pits on the inner surface, surrounded by hairs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Trapped humid air reduces the water vapour gradient, so less water is lost while some gas exchange continues. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to adaptations that reduce transpiration.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Stomata are the most important adaptation for controlling water loss in plants."
items.answer: Stomata provide the main dynamic control, but the cuticle and structural and physiological adaptations are also essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stomata can close quickly to reduce water loss when water is scarce; transpiration occurs mainly through stomata. Arguments against: the waxy cuticle prevents most water loss from the leaf surface; other adaptations such as leaf rolling, CAM and small leaves also reduce water loss. Supported judgement: Stomata provide the main dynamic control, but the cuticle and structural and physiological adaptations are also essential.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Loosely packed leaf cells with large air spaces that allow diffusion of gases to and from photosynthesising cells"?
items.answer: spongy mesophyll
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of spongy mesophyll.

items.stem: Why does wind increase transpiration rate?
options: It removes water vapour from around the leaf, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient.
items.answer: It removes water vapour from around the leaf, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient.
items.markingKey: C. Removes the boundary layer.

items.stem: In a potometer the air bubble moved 45 mm in 5 minutes in a capillary of radius 0.5 mm. What is the rate of water uptake?
items.answer: 7.1 mm³ min⁻¹

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "cardiac cycle".
items.answer: The sequence of events in one heartbeat, including atrial and ventricular systole and diastole
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the sequence of events in one heartbeat, including atrial and ventricular systole and diastole. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Isabel writes: "The heartbeat is started by nerve impulses from the brain." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Cardiac muscle is myogenic: the SA node initiates each beat; nerves and hormones only change the rate.
items.markingKey: Cardiac muscle is myogenic: the SA node initiates each beat; nerves and hormones only change the rate. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how the structure of arteries is related to their function.
items.answer: Thick walls with collagen withstand high pressure; elastic fibres stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, maintaining pressure and smoothing flow; smooth muscle can constrict or dilate to regulate flow; narrow lumen maintains pressure. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Thick walls with collagen withstand high pressure; elastic fibres stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, maintaining pressure and smoothing flow; smooth muscle can constrict or dilate to regulate flow; narrow lumen maintains pressure. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Stroke volume is 70 cm³ and heart rate 72 beats min⁻¹. What is the cardiac output?
items.answer: 5.04 dm³ min⁻¹

items.stem: An ECG of Kwame shows that the time between successive R waves is 0.67 s. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute. The stroke volume is 72 cm³. Calculate the cardiac output in dm³ min⁻¹.
items.answer: 90 beats min⁻¹; 6.45 dm³ min⁻¹

items.stem:
A bubble potometer (capillary radius 0.5 mm) was used to measure water uptake by a leafy shoot under different conditions. The distance moved by the bubble in 5 minutes was recorded three times for each condition.

Condition | Distance 1 / mm | Distance 2 / mm | Distance 3 / mm
still air, 20 °C | 25 | 22 | 22
fan (moving air), 20 °C | 62 | 55 | 55
still air, 30 °C | 48 | 42 | 47
plastic bag over shoot, 20 °C | 7 | 8 | 7
dark, 20 °C | 4 | 4 | 4

(a) Calculate the mean distance moved for “still air, 30 °C”. [1]
(b) Calculate the rate of water uptake for “still air, 30 °C” in mm³ min⁻¹. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage change in mean distance when the fan was switched on. [2]
(d) Explain the effect of moving air on the rate of transpiration. [2]
items.answer: (a) 45.7 mm (b) 7.2 mm³ min⁻¹ (c) +149.3 % (d) Moving air removes water vapour from around the stomata, maintaining a steep water vapour gradient, so diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf is faster.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 48 + 42 + 47 ÷ 3 = 45.7 mm (A1). (b) [2] π × 0.5² × 45.7 = 35.9 mm³ (M1); ÷ 5 = 7.2 (A1). (c) [2] (57.3 − 23.0)/23.0 × 100 (M1) = +149.3 % (A1). (d) [2] Removes humid air/boundary layer (A1); steeper gradient → faster diffusion (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Coronary heart disease is mainly caused by lifestyle factors."
items.answer: Lifestyle factors are major modifiable contributors, but genetics and age also play substantial roles; risk results from their interaction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: smoking, high saturated fat diet, lack of exercise and obesity raise risk; risk falls when people change these behaviours. Arguments against: genetic factors such as familial hypercholesterolaemia strongly affect risk; age and sex are non-modifiable risk factors. Supported judgement: Lifestyle factors are major modifiable contributors, but genetics and age also play substantial roles; risk results from their interaction.

items.stem: Describe the events of the cardiac cycle, including pressure changes and valve movements, and explain how the heartbeat is controlled.
items.answer: Atrial systole: AV valves open, ventricles fill. Ventricular systole: AV close, pressure rises, SL open, ejection. Diastole: SL close, filling. SA node pacemaker, AV delay, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres; myogenic; nerves/adrenaline alter rate; ECG.
items.markingKey: Atrial systole: AV valves open, ventricles fill. Ventricular systole: AV close, pressure rises, SL open, ejection. Diastole: SL close, filling. SA node pacemaker, AV delay, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres; myogenic; nerves/adrenaline alter rate; ECG.

items.stem: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than that of the right ventricle?
options: It holds a larger volume of blood.
It pumps blood to the lungs.
It must generate higher pressure to pump blood around the whole body.
items.answer: It must generate higher pressure to pump blood around the whole body.
items.markingKey: D. Systemic circulation has higher resistance.

items.stem: Explain the difference between veins and arteries.
items.answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, with thick muscular elastic walls and narrow lumens; veins return blood at low pressure, with thinner walls, wide lumens and valves.
items.markingKey: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, with thick muscular elastic walls and narrow lumens; veins return blood at low pressure, with thinner walls, wide lumens and valves. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using occlusion of a coronary artery in a heart attack as an example, explain the importance of blood supply to cardiac muscle.
items.answer: A blood clot on an atherosclerotic plaque blocks a coronary artery, cutting off blood to part of the heart muscle. Without oxygen, cardiac muscle cells cannot respire aerobically and die, reducing the heart’s ability to pump.
items.markingKey: Context (A blood clot on an atherosclerotic plaque blocks a coronary artery, cutting off blood to part of the heart muscle.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without oxygen, cardiac muscle cells cannot respire aerobically and die, reducing the heart’s ability to pump. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of blood supply to cardiac muscle.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A hard polymer deposited in xylem walls that strengthens them and resists collapse under tension"?
items.answer: lignin
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of lignin.

items.stem: Explain how root pressure is generated.
items.answer: Root cells actively transport mineral ions into the xylem; water potential in the xylem falls; water enters by osmosis from surrounding cells; pressure builds up and pushes water up the xylem, especially when transpiration is low.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Root cells actively transport mineral ions into the xylem; water potential in the xylem falls; water enters by osmosis from surrounding cells; pressure builds up and pushes water up the xylem, especially when transpiration is low. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why can xylem vessels conduct water efficiently?
options: They are dead, hollow tubes with no end walls or cytoplasm.
items.answer: They are dead, hollow tubes with no end walls or cytoplasm.
items.markingKey: A. Continuous columns of water.

items.stem: Outline one way in which aphids feeding on phloem sap shows the pressure-flow mechanism of translocation.
items.answer: Aphid mouthparts (stylets) penetrate single sieve tubes; when the aphid is cut away, sap continues to exude from the stylet under pressure. The exudation shows phloem contents are under positive pressure and allows sap to be sampled and analysed.
items.markingKey: Context (Aphid mouthparts (stylets) penetrate single sieve tubes; when the aphid is cut away, sap continues to exude from the stylet under pressure.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The exudation shows phloem contents are under positive pressure and allows sap to be sampled and analysed. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the pressure-flow mechanism of translocation.

items.stem: The diameter of a tree trunk changed from 542.9 mm at dawn to 540.6 mm at midday. Calculate the percentage change and suggest a biological explanation for it.
items.answer: -0.4 %; tension in the xylem during rapid transpiration pulls the walls inward, slightly shrinking the trunk.
items.markingKey: % change = (540.6 − 542.9)/542.9 × 100 (M1) = -0.4 % (A1). Explanation (R1): tension in the xylem during rapid transpiration pulls the walls inward, slightly shrinking the trunk.

items.stem: Compare the structure and function of xylem and phloem and explain how water and sugars are transported in plants.
items.answer: Xylem: dead, lignified, continuous, pits; transpiration pull, cohesion–tension, root pressure. Phloem: sieve tubes, sieve plates, companion cells; active loading, osmosis, hydrostatic pressure, source to sink; aphid evidence; bidirectional.
items.markingKey: Xylem: dead, lignified, continuous, pits; transpiration pull, cohesion–tension, root pressure. Phloem: sieve tubes, sieve plates, companion cells; active loading, osmosis, hydrostatic pressure, source to sink; aphid evidence; bidirectional.

items.stem: Which cells take up water and mineral ions from the soil?
items.answer: root hair cells
items.markingKey: C. Large surface area.

items.stem: A student claims: "Phloem always carries sugar downwards from leaves to roots." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Phloem carries sugar from sources to sinks, which can be up (to growing shoots, fruits) or down.
items.markingKey: Phloem carries sugar from sources to sinks, which can be up (to growing shoots, fruits) or down. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The pressure-flow hypothesis fully explains translocation in phloem." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Pressure flow is the best-supported explanation, but some observations suggest it may not account for all details of translocation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: active loading at sources and osmotic pressure explain flow from source to sink; aphid stylet experiments confirm pressure in sieve tubes. Arguments against: different solutes have been observed moving at different speeds in the same sieve tube; the role of sieve plates and possible active mechanisms along the pathway are debated. Supported judgement: Pressure flow is the best-supported explanation, but some observations suggest it may not account for all details of translocation. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Define the term "sliding filament model".
items.answer: The model in which muscle contraction occurs as myosin heads pull actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere, shortening it without the filaments themselves shortening
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the model in which muscle contraction occurs as myosin heads pull actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere, shortening it without the filaments themselves shortening. items.stem: Why are muscles arranged in antagonistic pairs?
options: Muscles can only pull by contracting, so a second muscle is needed to reverse the movement.
items.answer: Muscles can only pull by contracting, so a second muscle is needed to reverse the movement.
items.markingKey: C. E.g. biceps flexes, triceps extends.

items.stem: A student claims: "During contraction the actin and myosin filaments get shorter." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The filaments stay the same length; they slide past each other so that the sarcomere shortens.
items.markingKey: The filaments stay the same length; they slide past each other so that the sarcomere shortens. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An electron micrograph of a myofibril at × 30000 shows a sarcomere 69.6 mm long. Calculate the actual length of the sarcomere in µm.
Outline one way in which rigor mortis used in forensic science shows the role of ATP in the cross-bridge cycle.
items.answer: Muscles stiffen 2–6 hours after death and relax after 24–48 hours as proteins break down. Without ATP, myosin heads stay bound to actin, locking muscles until the proteins degrade.
items.markingKey: Context (Muscles stiffen 2–6 hours after death and relax after 24–48 hours as proteins break down.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without ATP, myosin heads stay bound to actin, locking muscles until the proteins degrade. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of ATP in the cross-bridge cycle.

items.stem: Describe the structure of a sarcomere and explain how muscle contraction occurs.
items.answer: Z lines, actin (thin), myosin (thick), A band, I band, H zone, M line, titin. Impulse → Ca²⁺ from SR → troponin/tropomyosin → cross-bridges → power stroke (ADP + Pi released) → ATP detaches → hydrolysis re-cocks → sarcomere shortens; A band constant; antagonistic pairs; relaxation via Ca²⁺ pumping.
items.markingKey: Z lines, actin (thin), myosin (thick), A band, I band, H zone, M line, titin. Impulse → Ca²⁺ from SR → troponin/tropomyosin → cross-bridges → power stroke (ADP + Pi released) → ATP detaches → hydrolysis re-cocks → sarcomere shortens; A band constant; antagonistic pairs; relaxation via Ca²⁺ pumping.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The model in which muscle contraction occurs as myosin heads pull actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere, shortening it without the filaments themselves shortening"?
items.answer: sliding filament model

items.stem: A sarcomere shortens from 2.4 µm to 1.8 µm. The A band is 1.6 µm. What is the length of each half I band after contraction?
items.answer: 0.1 µm
items.markingKey: D. I band total = 1.8 − 1.6 = 0.2 µm, so 0.1 µm each side.

items.stem: "The sliding filament model is fully supported by evidence." Discuss.
items.answer: The core model is extremely well supported; ongoing research refines details rather than challenging it.

items.answer: The volume of air breathed in or out in one normal breath, about 0.5 dm³ at rest

items.stem: Which tissue layer of a leaf has the most chloroplasts?
items.answer: palisade mesophyll

items.stem: Explain the difference between xylem and phloem.
items.answer: Xylem: dead lignified vessels, water and minerals, one direction (roots to leaves), driven by transpiration tension; phloem: living sieve tubes with companion cells, sucrose and amino acids, bidirectional from sources to sinks, driven by active loading and pressure.

items.stem: Explain the sliding filament model of muscle contraction.
items.answer: A nerve impulse causes Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca²⁺ binds troponin, moving tropomyosin off actin binding sites; myosin heads (energised by ATP hydrolysis) bind to actin forming cross-bridges; the power stroke pulls actin towards the M line; ATP binds, heads detach and re-cock; repeated cycles shorten the sarcomere.

(2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between expiration at rest and inspiration.
items.answer: In inspiration the diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume increases and pressure falls; in resting expiration these muscles relax, elastic recoil decreases volume and increases pressure, forcing air out.
items.markingKey: In inspiration the diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume increases and pressure falls; in resting expiration these muscles relax, elastic recoil decreases volume and increases pressure, forcing air out. items.stem: Why does blood pressure fall as blood passes from arteries to capillaries?
options: The total cross-sectional area increases and friction with vessel walls dissipates energy.
Blood is lost from the circulation.
items.answer: The total cross-sectional area increases and friction with vessel walls dissipates energy.
items.markingKey: A. Many narrow vessels in parallel.

items.stem: Distinguish between palisade mesophyll and spongy mesophyll.
items.answer: Palisade mesophyll is tightly packed columnar cells with many chloroplasts, specialised for photosynthesis; spongy mesophyll is loosely packed with large air spaces for gas diffusion and fewer chloroplasts.
items.markingKey: Palisade mesophyll is tightly packed columnar cells with many chloroplasts, specialised for photosynthesis; spongy mesophyll is loosely packed with large air spaces for gas diffusion and fewer chloroplasts. With reference to emphysema in long-term smokers, explain how it illustrates the importance of alveolar structure for gas exchange.
items.answer: Elastase from inflammatory cells breaks down elastin in alveolar walls, which merge into large air spaces. Reduced surface area and loss of elastic recoil lower the efficiency of gas exchange and ventilation.
items.markingKey: Context (Elastase from inflammatory cells breaks down elastin in alveolar walls, which merge into large air spaces.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Reduced surface area and loss of elastic recoil lower the efficiency of gas exchange and ventilation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of alveolar structure for gas exchange.

items.stem: At rest Felix has a heart rate of 58 beats min⁻¹ and a stroke volume of 62 cm³. During intense exercise these become 171 beats min⁻¹ and 103 cm³. Calculate the cardiac output in each case and the factor by which it increases.
items.answer: 3.60 and 17.61 dm³ min⁻¹; × 4.9

items.stem: In a bubble potometer with a shoot of a tomato plant in still air at 20 °C, the air bubble moved 93 mm in 2 minutes along a capillary tube of internal radius 0.4 mm. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹.
items.answer: 23.4 mm³ min⁻¹

items.stem: A ring of bark (including phloem) is removed from a tree trunk. After some weeks the bark just above the ring swells. Why?
options: Water accumulates because xylem is cut.
Sugars transported downwards in phloem accumulate above the cut.
items.answer: Sugars transported downwards in phloem accumulate above the cut.
items.markingKey: B. Phloem is outside the xylem.

items.stem: "During contraction the actin and myosin filaments get shorter." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The filaments stay the same length; they slide past each other so that the sarcomere shortens.
items.markingKey: The filaments stay the same length; they slide past each other so that the sarcomere shortens. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ana’s tidal volume sitting reading was 0.5 dm³ at 15 breaths per minute. During exercise it was 1.97 dm³ at 34 breaths per minute. Calculate the ventilation rate in each case and the percentage increase, and explain why it increases.
items.answer: 7.50 → 67.0 dm³ min⁻¹; +793 %; respiration in muscles increases, so more CO₂ must be removed and more O₂ supplied – rising blood CO₂ is detected by chemoreceptors, which increase breathing rate and depth
items.markingKey: 7.50 and 67.0 dm³ min⁻¹ (A1 A1); (67.0 − 7.50)/7.50 × 100 = 793 % (A1); more CO₂ from respiration detected by chemoreceptors, more O₂ needed (R1).

Explain how leaves are adapted for gas exchange and describe how the rate of transpiration can be measured and affected by abiotic factors.
items.answer: Leaf adaptations; stomata, guard cells; potometer: cut under water, seal, bubble, rate = πr²d/t; factors: light (stomata open), temperature, humidity, wind; trade-off; stomatal density measurement by nail varnish impressions.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The pressure-flow hypothesis fully explains translocation in phloem."
items.answer: Pressure flow is the best-supported explanation, but some observations suggest it may not account for all details of translocation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: active loading at sources and osmotic pressure explain flow from source to sink; aphid stylet experiments confirm pressure in sieve tubes. Arguments against: different solutes have been observed moving at different speeds in the same sieve tube; the role of sieve plates and possible active mechanisms along the pathway are debated. Supported judgement: Pressure flow is the best-supported explanation, but some observations suggest it may not account for all details of translocation. items.stem: "The sliding filament model is fully supported by evidence." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The core model is extremely well supported; ongoing research refines details rather than challenging it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: electron micrographs show A band length constant while I band and H zone shorten; X-ray diffraction and single-molecule studies show myosin power strokes. Arguments against: the elastic role of titin and other proteins was discovered later; details of force generation by myosin are still being studied. Supported judgement: The core model is extremely well supported; ongoing research refines details rather than challenging it. items.stem: What happens to pressure inside the thorax during inspiration?
items.answer: it decreases below atmospheric pressure
items.markingKey: B. Air flows in down the pressure gradient.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The sequence of events in one heartbeat, including atrial and ventricular systole and diastole"?
items.answer: cardiac cycle
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of cardiac cycle.

items.stem: Where are most stomata found on the leaves of typical dicotyledonous plants?
items.answer: on the lower (abaxial) surface
items.markingKey: on the lower (abaxial) surface. Reduces water loss from the sunlit upper surface.

items.stem: Diego writes: "Phloem always carries sugar downwards from leaves to roots." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Phloem carries sugar from sources to sinks, which can be up (to growing shoots, fruits) or down.
items.markingKey: Phloem carries sugar from sources to sinks, which can be up (to growing shoots, fruits) or down. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the I band and the A band.
items.answer: The A band contains myosin (with overlapping actin) and stays the same length; the I band contains actin only and shortens during contraction.
items.markingKey: The A band contains myosin (with overlapping actin) and stays the same length; the I band contains actin only and shortens during contraction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "During inspiration air is sucked in, which pushes the ribs out." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Muscle contraction expands the thorax first; the drop in pressure then causes air to flow in.
items.markingKey: Muscle contraction expands the thorax first; the drop in pressure then causes air to flow in. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between systole and diastole.
items.answer: Systole is contraction of heart chambers that ejects blood; diastole is relaxation during which chambers fill.
items.markingKey: Systole is contraction of heart chambers that ejects blood; diastole is relaxation during which chambers fill. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how temperature affects the rate of transpiration.
items.answer: Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, so evaporation from mesophyll cell walls and diffusion of water vapour out through stomata are faster; warm air holds more water vapour, so the gradient is steeper.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, so evaporation from mesophyll cell walls and diffusion of water vapour out through stomata are faster; warm air holds more water vapour, so the gradient is steeper. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: How is a high pressure generated in the phloem at a source?
options: Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes, lowering water potential so water enters by osmosis.
items.answer: Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes, lowering water potential so water enters by osmosis.
items.markingKey: C. Pressure-flow mechanism.

items.stem: In an electron micrograph at × 25 000, a sarcomere measures 62.5 mm. What is its actual length?
items.answer: 2.5 µm

items.answer: 80 beats min⁻¹

items.stem: Outline one way in which marram grass (Ammophila arenaria) on sand dunes shows adaptations that reduce transpiration.
items.answer: Its leaves roll up in dry conditions with stomata in pits on the inner surface, surrounded by hairs. Trapped humid air reduces the water vapour gradient, so less water is lost while some gas exchange continues.
items.markingKey: Context (Its leaves roll up in dry conditions with stomata in pits on the inner surface, surrounded by hairs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Trapped humid air reduces the water vapour gradient, so less water is lost while some gas exchange continues. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to adaptations that reduce transpiration.

items.stem: With reference to ringing experiments on woody stems, explain how it illustrates the role of phloem in translocation.
items.answer: Removing a ring of bark causes swelling above the ring as sugars accumulate. Phloem lies in the bark; cutting it stops downward transport of sugar while xylem transport continues.
items.markingKey: Context (Removing a ring of bark causes swelling above the ring as sugars accumulate.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Phloem lies in the bark; cutting it stops downward transport of sugar while xylem transport continues. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of phloem in translocation.

items.stem: A relaxed sarcomere is 2.26 µm long and its A band is 1.6 µm. During contraction the sarcomere shortens to 1.69 µm. Calculate the percentage shortening of the sarcomere and the total length of I band before and after contraction, and explain why the A band does not change.
items.answer: 25.2 % shorter; I band 0.66 → 0.09 µm; A band = length of myosin, which does not shorten
items.markingKey: (2.26 − 1.69)/2.26 × 100 = 25.2 % (A1); I = sarcomere − A: 0.66 and 0.09 µm (A1 A1); filaments slide, myosin length constant (R1).

items.stem: With reference to surfactant therapy for premature infants, explain how it illustrates the role of type II pneumocytes.
items.answer: Babies born before about 30 weeks are given artificial surfactant through a tube into the trachea. Supplying surfactant lowers surface tension so alveoli stay inflated and gas exchange can occur.
items.markingKey: Context (Babies born before about 30 weeks are given artificial surfactant through a tube into the trachea.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Supplying surfactant lowers surface tension so alveoli stay inflated and gas exchange can occur. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of type II pneumocytes.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Coronary heart disease is mainly caused by lifestyle factors."
items.answer: Lifestyle factors are major modifiable contributors, but genetics and age also play substantial roles; risk results from their interaction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: smoking, high saturated fat diet, lack of exercise and obesity raise risk; risk falls when people change these behaviours. Arguments against: genetic factors such as familial hypercholesterolaemia strongly affect risk; age and sex are non-modifiable risk factors. Supported judgement: Lifestyle factors are major modifiable contributors, but genetics and age also play substantial roles; risk results from their interaction.

items.stem: "Stomata are the most important adaptation for controlling water loss in plants." Discuss.
items.answer: Stomata provide the main dynamic control, but the cuticle and structural and physiological adaptations are also essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stomata can close quickly to reduce water loss when water is scarce; transpiration occurs mainly through stomata. Arguments against: the waxy cuticle prevents most water loss from the leaf surface; other adaptations such as leaf rolling, CAM and small leaves also reduce water loss. Supported judgement: Stomata provide the main dynamic control, but the cuticle and structural and physiological adaptations are also essential. items.stem:
A bubble potometer (capillary radius 0.5 mm) was used to measure water uptake by a leafy shoot under different conditions. The distance moved by the bubble in 5 minutes was recorded three times for each condition.

Condition | Distance 1 / mm | Distance 2 / mm | Distance 3 / mm
still air, 20 °C | 23 | 25 | 24
fan (moving air), 20 °C | 56 | 52 | 52
still air, 30 °C | 37 | 37 | 36
plastic bag over shoot, 20 °C | 8 | 7 | 8
dark, 20 °C | 5 | 5 | 5

(a) Calculate the mean distance moved for “still air, 30 °C”. [1]
(b) Calculate the rate of water uptake for “still air, 30 °C” in mm³ min⁻¹. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage change in mean distance when the fan was switched on. [2]
(d) Explain the effect of moving air on the rate of transpiration. [2]
(e) Explain the results for the shoot covered with a plastic bag and the shoot in the dark. [2]
(f) State two precautions needed when setting up a potometer. [2]
(g) Explain why the potometer measures water uptake rather than transpiration. [1]
items.answer: (a) 36.7 mm (b) 5.8 mm³ min⁻¹ (c) +122.2 % (d) Moving air removes water vapour from around the stomata, maintaining a steep water vapour gradient, so diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf is faster. (e) Bag: humidity rises, reducing the diffusion gradient; dark: stomata close, so little water vapour escapes. (f) Cut the shoot under water; ensure the apparatus is airtight/no air bubbles in xylem; dry the leaves; allow time to equilibrate. (g) Some water absorbed is used in photosynthesis or to maintain turgor, so uptake is not exactly equal to water lost.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 37 + 37 + 36 ÷ 3 = 36.7 mm (A1). (b) [2] π × 0.5² × 36.7 = 28.8 mm³ (M1); ÷ 5 = 5.8 (A1). (c) [2] (53.3 − 24.0)/24.0 × 100 (M1) = +122.2 % (A1). (d) [2] Removes humid air/boundary layer (A1); steeper gradient → faster diffusion (A1). (e) [2] Bag – high humidity/low gradient (A1); dark – stomata close (A1). (f) [2] Two valid precautions (A1 A1). (g) [1] Water used by cells (A1).
